extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in journalism, mass communication, and media studies; practicing journalists and news editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for assessing journalistic practice (standards, sourcing, editing, and manipulations) and for designing media-content and media-effects research that integrates content variables and contingent conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of newsworthiness, accuracy, and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic work should be judged by the integrity of the work—whether it meets accepted standards of newsworthiness, accuracy, and fairness—rather than the reporter's personal beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors will typically defend a reporter against charges if 'all the minor facts' are right; integrity of reporting is the metric by which ideological commitments are to be judged (MacDougall; Columbia Journalism Review editorial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity and impartiality; avoid shrill/propagandistic tone and personal opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should adhere to professional codes of objectivity and impartiality and avoid being shrill, propagandistic, or stating personal opinion in their reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mainstream outlets may tolerate diverse viewpoints so long as the reporter 'adheres to the readily assimilated professional code of objectivity and impartiality and doesn't violate canons against being shrill and propagandistic or stating a personal opinion' (MacDougall example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance in sourcing (provide opposing viewpoints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should include opposing or mainstream spokespeople to provide balance and confer respectability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may require that a conservative or opposing spokesperson be quoted to balance a story (example: editor made MacDougall introduce a conservative spokesman to balance an inequality story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance, controversy, color, and surprise for commercial relevance/readability
rubrics_metrics.description: To meet commercial journalistic standards of relevance and readability, pieces should contain elements of significance, controversy, color, and surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MacDougall claimed his stories contained enough of these attributes to satisfy commercial standards; such attributes make material acceptable to editors concerned with readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: calm, matter-of-fact, non-polemical presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when covering contested or value-laden topics, reporting should be calm, matter-of-fact, and non-polemical in tone to fit professional formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A non-polemical tone helps radical or divergent perspectives pass editorial review (MacDougall's strategy and editors' expectations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid manipulating or staging events/images (no manufactured news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and photojournalists must not stage or manipulate events/images; manipulating the situation is equivalent to manipulating the news and breaches professional norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: LA Times photographer Mike Meadows was suspended for staging a photograph; editor's comment: 'When you manipulate the situation, you manipulate the news.' Even 'harmless' manipulations can be punished to preserve institutional myths about journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing routines as safeguards against reporter bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Robust editing processes and newsroom routines are expected to filter out reporter bias before publication and are invoked to defend newsroom credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions (e.g., Dow Jones) point to their editing process as evidence that bias was removed; senior editors and managing editors defend reporters by citing thorough editing and review routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing practices that intentionally select supporting experts (identified as problematic tactic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting experts known to support a preordained thesis, and using mainstream authorities to confer respectability on radical views, is a practiced tactic used by some reporters but is seen as ethically questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MacDougall admitted seeking experts who would support his thesis and using mainstream authorities to give recognition to radical views; industry reaction framed this as a challenge to journalistic credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational responses to paradigm violations (repair strategies)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a journalist violates newsroom paradigm norms, organizations use repair strategies: (1) disengage and distance the reporter's values from their work, (2) reassert the effectiveness of routines (editing) to prevent distortion, and (3) marginalize the person and/or message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: public statements distancing values, letters asserting editing safeguards (Dow Jones), rhetorical marginalization of the reporter's role or credibility in trade and popular press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include media content variables when studying media effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Media-effects research should not ignore the content itself; studies must incorporate variables describing media content and the factors that shape it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book argues that borrowing theories from other disciplines without including content leads to oversimplified conclusions; integrating content fosters better theory-building in mass communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure exposure to specific content rather than exposure to a medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should measure individuals' exposure to particular content (e.g., violent scenes, public-affairs stories) rather than using coarse measures like hours of TV or days-per-week newspaper readership as proxies for content exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Heavy TV viewers could avoid violent content despite many hours watched; a daily newspaper reader might only read comics/sports, not public affairs—thus exposure-to-medium is not equivalent to exposure-to-content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider media characteristics, media workers, and environment as contingent conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining content-effects relationships, treat characteristics of the media, production companies, media workers, and the wider environment as contingent variables that moderate effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domains A–E model: e.g., Palmgreen & Clarke showed agenda-setting may differ between newspapers and local TV; production-company differences can explain differential effects of similar-appearing violent content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop precise and valid measures of content sensitive to qualitative differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Content measures must go beyond coarse indices (e.g., simple violence counts) to capture qualitative attributes that may matter for effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gerbner's violence index can give identical scores for shows whose violence differs in type or context; more sophisticated measures are needed to detect important differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include audience use as an intervening variable where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies should model audience use/exposure as an intervening mechanism between content characteristics and effects rather than assuming exposure always occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domains B–E discussions (e.g., cultivation research) treat overall exposure as the intervening variable; authors recommend explicitly measuring use to improve inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ fully elaborated models (A-B-C-D-E) when appropriate to capture direct and indirect effects
rubrics_metrics.description: To best understand mass communication, use integrated models that allow for direct effects of content, intervening audience use, and contingent conditions from media and audience characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The A-B-C-D-E model captures direct and inferred effects, media influences, audience characteristics, and intervening use; it supports richer theory and explanation of how content shapes social reality.
